    ADHD Medications May Improve Brain Fog in Perimenopausal Women: Fresh Research

    📅 23 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1320 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Additudemag

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Preliminary evidence indicates self-reported brain fog decreases and executive function improves in perimenopausal women treated with ADHD medications.
    • Stimulant and non-stimulant medications used to treat ADHD significantly improve self-reported executive dysfunction in perimenopausal women without ADHD, according to preliminary evidence presented at the annual meeting of The Menopause Society last month in San Diego.
    • During the presentation titled “Brain Fog or ADHD?
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Preliminary evidence indicates self-reported brain fog decreases and executive function improves in perimenopausal women treated with ADHD medications.

    Stimulant and non-stimulant medications used to treat ADHD significantly improve self-reported executive dysfunction in perimenopausal women without ADHD, according to preliminary evidence presented at the annual meeting of The Menopause Society last month in San Diego. (These findings have not yet been published in a peer-reviewed journal.)1.

    During the presentation titled “Brain Fog or ADHD? Executive Dysfunction in Perimenopause: A Scoping Review of the Role of ADHD Medications,” researchers discussed the effectiveness of two ADHD medications: lisdexamphetamine (brand name: Vyvanse), a stimulant, and atomoxetine, a non-stimulant. They studied the impact of these medications on cognition and ADHD symptom severity in women aged 45 to 60 years during the perimenopausal period. The systematic review included three crossover randomized controlled trials involving 60 patients and two cross-sectional studies of 6,048 patients from Iceland and the U.K.

    The study found that both lisdexamphetamine (LDX) and atomoxetine (ATX) significantly improve self-reported executive dysfunction, as measured by the Brown Attention Deficit Disorder Scale (BADDS), a self-report rating scale that measures ADHD symptoms, compared to placebo. The BADDS scores for LDX users dropped from 35.7 to 21.2, compared to 29.8 with placebo. The BADDS scores for ATX users fell from 38.6 to 25.5, compared to 30.1 with placebo. Neuroimaging data from a subset of women taking LDX further supports these findings.

    Recent findings suggest that during perimenopause, declining or fluctuating estrogen levels affect dopamine and norepinephrine signaling in the prefrontal cortex of the brain. As a result, many perimenopausal women experience “brain fog,” which is an umbrella term for forgetfulness, slow thinking, difficulty finding words, and reduced concentration, which can also be a symptom of ADHD. This overlap often leaves clinicians trying to discern whether a patient’s brain fog stems from hormonal fluctuations or undiagnosed ADHD, or both.

    “Many women at perimenopause notice changes in focus, memory, and organization that look a lot like ADHD, and the two can be hard to tell apart,” said lead author Jennifer Tat, M.D. candidate and fourth-year medical student at the University of Tennessee Health Science Center in Memphis.

    It has been revealed that in an ADDitude survey of more than 5,000 women with diagnosed and undiagnosed ADHD, 94% of survey respondents stated their ADHD symptoms grew more severe during perimenopause and menopause. During this stage, respondents said the most impactful ADHD symptoms were brain fog or memory problems, and overwhelm, both of which 70% of women said had a “life-altering impact” in their 40s and 50s.

    It has been revealed that “Brain fog became unmanageable,” wrote one 45-year-old mother of two who entered perimenopause at age 41. “Distractibility increased and my inability to complete work tasks in an appropriate amount of time decreased. I began spending all night working just to keep up. Things that I used to have unconscious strategies to deal with were no longer manageable.”.

    It has been revealed that “I never experienced rage or brain fog before perimenopause,” wrote one woman. “Overwhelm has been more frequent in recent years, and depression began in my 40s. I definitely attribute some of this to hormonal changes.”.

    Industry observers note that “In perimenopause, the brain fog and memory, inattention, distractibility, perfectionism, hyperactivity, and restlessness problems become progressively worse,” wrote a 52-year-old woman diagnosed with ADHD at age 50. “I have always had these symptoms, but I was able to manage them with systems that I created for myself. My ability to manage them has declined significantly, and this makes these symptoms seem like they are the worst they have ever been.”.

    While preliminary evidence from the systematic review found ADHD medications improve subjective executive function, the medications had little to no significant impact on objective cognitive measures, according to tests measuring working memory and sustained attention.

    Prior research suggests otherwise.

    In the ADDitude article “Could ADHD Medications Improve Memory, Focus & Organization in Menopausal Women? The Research Says Yes,” the late Thomas E. Brown, Ph.D., described how his research with C. Neill Epperson, M.D., found ADHD medications alleviated cognitive problems resembling ADHD symptoms in menopausal women without ADHD.

    The series of three studies measured symptoms with BADDS, which Brown developed. The first study found that ATX treatment significantly improved BADDS scores for working memory; focus scores improved in BADDS scores for women treated with ATX.2 In the second study, executive functions improved, including an objective measure of short-term working memory, in 41% of menopausal women taking 20 to 60 mg LDX daily, compared to 17% for the women on the placebo.3 The third study examined the effects of LDX on the brain functioning of women with no history of ADHD, but with reported cognitive difficulties with working memory, organization, focus, and attention that had begun during menopause.4.

    “As predicted, neuroimaging data revealed that LDX activated executive networks in specific areas of the brain,” Brown wrote. “Those data also showed that LDX’s effect on specific brain regions was associated with improved BADDS scores overall, and with BADDS scores for activation and alertness/effort. Imaging data indicated that improvements in brain activation were significantly larger when women were on LDX than when they were on placebo.”.

    The studies were published in peer-reviewed medical journals in 2011, 2015, and 2017; however, Brown wrote in 2021, “results of that research have not yet been widely recognized.”.

    There is at the moment no FDA-approved pharmacological intervention for executive dysfunction and brain fog during perimenopause or menopause. Research on the most effective treatments for ADHD during perimenopause is limited as well. That said, Patricia Quinn, M.D., explained during a 2026 ADDitude webinar that available data and observational evidence suggest that many women could benefit from estrogen supplementation and increased stimulant dosages during this phase.

    “Perimenopause is when you need the most help, the most support,” Quinn said in her webinar, “Perimenopause in Women with ADHD.” “Estrogen… makes your stimulant more effective.”.

    Industry observers note that one roadblock to care is the fact that many healthcare professionals are ill-equipped to provide responsive, coordinated, evidence-based treatment and support to help women navigate menopause, according to a study published in The Lancet Obstetrics, Gynecology, & Women’s Health. The 2026 study cited inadequate medical training, paltry research, and persistent gaps in knowledge as reasons for the “fragmented care.”5.

    Combined, these preliminary findings could open the door to a nonhormone therapeutic option for addressing perimenopausal executive dysfunction, according to researcher Tat.

    According to recent reports, “Our review found early signs that ADHD medications may help women feel more on top of their daily lives,” Tat remarked. “While it’s too early to recommend these medications, a quick screen for ADHD symptoms is a simple step that could help women get the right care.”.

    Mutabor builds the Voith brand identity around movement: a V-Vector symbol, a custom typeface, and a blue made for screens.

    According to recent reports, the whole system starts with a single chevron. Mutabor calls it the V-Vector, a > that points forward and never sits still: it repeats into a pattern on the Appleton reception wall, frames a machine on the launch poster, and turns into punctuation inside the headlines. Voith Blue stays the signature color, and bright tones join it, a vivid royal blue for screens and a mint green for the accent word. On black, "Machines with a digital heart." puts the machine inside the chevron. On blue, "Always breaking new ground" lets the green >ground do the talking.

    The custom typeface carries the voice. Mutabor drew it only for Voith, and it reveals in the way headlines sit: heavy, round, and set large enough that one line fills a poster. "Hydro driving renewable momentum" runs white on blue with the green >momentum as the punchline, and "Speed press" splits across a dark panel in the same weight. The VOITH wordmark stays in solid capitals, unchanged, while the type around it changes scale.

    One frame shows the construction behind it, a lowercase a drawn with node points and thin rules beside a turbine, the letter treated like an engineered part. The grid is visible in the letterform, and the same precision runs through the system, from the wordmark lockup to the small labels on the machine diagrams.

    According to recent reports, the system proves itself where the firm actually works. The reception wall at Appleton carries the blue V pattern behind "Welcome to Appleton", with the VOITH wordmark set into the desk. Posters, phone screens, documents, and an agenda share the same blue, the same green, and the same chevron, from a "We are hiring" phone card to a "CSH operating principle" diagram. A purple machine close-up is labeled "nanometer precision torque drive", the product photography sitting inside the same graphic language as the posters.

    Some of the case imagery is marked AI generated, Mutabor's own label on the frames, and the photography of the plants and machines reads as illustration as much as record. The rollout began in March 2026, after an internal launch in October 2025, and now runs across all markets and touchpoints. It is the first time the three business units, hydropower, papermaking, and drive technology, share one consistent, digitally native identity, and the work took the Red Dot Award for Corporate Design and Identity in 2026.

    • Sources indicate that navigating Attention Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) treatment options as an adult can feel overwhelming, but finding a treatment proposal that aligns with your specific health goals is an notable first step.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Exploring non-stimulant ADHD treatment? Use these questions to guide your next doctor discussion.

    Sources indicate that navigating Attention Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder (ADHD) treatment options as an adult can feel overwhelming, but finding a treatment proposal that aligns with your specific health goals is an notable first step. ADHD treatment isn’t one-size-fits-all. Non-stimulant treatments offer an option without controlled-substance management.

    Finding a treatment is a collaborative process. My role as a healthcare provider is to provide education and guidance to help patients make informed decisions about their care. As you explore whether non-stimulant options are the right fit for your daily routine, having clear, open communication is essential. To help guide a thoughtful, personalized conversation at your next doctor’s appointment, I’ve put together a list of key questions to help you get started. Dr. Jo Hughes is a paid consultant compensated by Supernus.

    Non-stimulants are noncontrolled prescription medications used to treat the core ADHD symptoms, inattention, hyperactivity, and/or impulsivity.

    With consistent daily dosing, non-stimulant medications can provide continuous medication exposure over a 24-hour period.

    Most non-stimulant medications offer a distinct and targeted approach to help manage daily ADHD symptoms, working gradually over time to improve symptom control.

    Every non-stimulant ADHD medication has a different safety profile, so side effects can vary. Having an open conversation with your provider before starting treatment is the best way to ensure your strategy fits your needs and daily routine.

    In a recent development, non-stimulants are noncontrolled medications. Talk to your doctor about prescription and refill options, including whether telehealth appointments are appropriate for you.

    Qelbree® (viloxazine extended-release capsules) is a convenient once-a-day non-stimulant ADHD medication for adults and kids ages 6 years and older. It was the first non-stimulant ADHD medication approved in over a decade with approximately 3 million prescriptions filled since launch in 2021 (for children 6-17 years old) and 2022 (in adults 18 years and older).

    Recent findings suggest that qelbree® (viloxazine extended-release capsules) is a prescription medicine used to treat ADHD in adults and children 6 years and older. Please click here for full Prescribing Information, including Boxed Warning, and Medication Guide.

    Qelbree may increase suicidal thoughts and actions in children and adults with ADHD, especially within the first few months of treatment or when the dose is changed. Tell your doctor if you or your child have (or if there is a family history of) suicidal thoughts or actions before starting Qelbree. Monitor your or your child’s moods, behaviors, thoughts, and feelings during treatment with Qelbree. Report any new or sudden changes in these symptoms right away.

    See below for full Key Safety Information.

    Beyond its established presence, Qelbree offers treatment versatility for patients with ADHD in a number of ways:.

    It has been revealed that finding an ADHD treatment can take time, there isn’t a one-size-fits all approach. Schedule time with your doctor to discuss all your options, including if Qelbree may be a good fit for you.

    To learn more, visit https://www.qelbree.com.

    ADDitude does not endorse any specific product, service, or treatment.

    Qelbree (viloxazine extended-release capsules) is a prescription medicine used to treat ADHD in adults and children 6 years and older.

    Qelbree may increase suicidal thoughts and actions, in children and adults with ADHD, especially within the first few months of treatment or when the dose is changed. Tell your doctor if you or your child have (or if there is a family history of) suicidal thoughts or actions before starting Qelbree. Monitor your or your child’s moods, behaviors, thoughts, and feelings during treatment with Qelbree. Report any fresh or sudden changes in these symptoms right away.

    According to recent reports, you should not take Qelbree if you or your child: Take a medicine for depression called a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI) or have stopped taking an MAOI in the past 14 days. Also, you or your child should avoid alosetron, duloxetine, ramelteon, tasimelteon, tizanidine, and theophylline.

    In a recent development, qelbree can increase blood pressure and heart rate. Your or your child’s doctor will monitor these vital signs.

    Qelbree may cause manic episodes in patients with bipolar disorder. Tell your doctor if you or your child show any signs of mania.

    It has been revealed that do not drive or operate heavy machinery until you know how Qelbree will affect you or your child. Qelbree may cause you or your child to feel sleepy or tired.

    The most common side effects of Qelbree in patients 6 to 17 years are sleepiness, not feeling hungry, feeling tired, nausea, vomiting, trouble sleeping, and irritability, and in adults, insomnia, headache, sleepiness, tiredness, nausea, decreased appetite, dry mouth, and constipation. These are not all the possible side effects of Qelbree.

    You are encouraged to report negative side effects of prescription drugs to the FDA.

    Visit www.fda.gov/medwatch or call 1-800-FDA-1088.

    Please see Medication Guide, including Boxed Warning.

    #160834. Does international art sell in India? Dealers at Art Mumbai encounter deep pockets but local tastes

    📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1436 w)
    📖 Baca
    General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Theartnewspaper ↗ Open Full Page

    Does international art sell in India? Dealers at Art Mumbai encounter deep pockets but local tastes

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1436 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

    ⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that india’s art market rally has not yet slowed, judging by the fourth edition of Art Mumbai, held from 12-15 November.
    • Sources indicate that the mushrooming wealth of India’s richest, who are shopping for major works to fill bigger homes, appears more than capable of sustaining its small but growing domestic base of galleries and auction houses.
    • Sources indicate that for India’s top galleries, success at Art Mumbai is now a foregone conclusion.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that india’s art market rally has not yet slowed, judging by the fourth edition of Art Mumbai, held from 12-15 November. While several Indian dealers noted that a date clash with Diwali had resulted in quieter VIP days than last year, this amounted to most local exhibitors selling around half, rather than all their stands.

    Sources indicate that the mushrooming wealth of India’s richest, who are shopping for major works to fill bigger homes, appears more than capable of sustaining its small but growing domestic base of galleries and auction houses. The country’s secondary art market recorded its best year ever in 2025, at $272.1m, according to a recent report by the wealth managers 360One (a sponsor of the fair).

    Sources indicate that for India’s top galleries, success at Art Mumbai is now a foregone conclusion. “This fair is great for us, and right now I feel more inclined to invest my effort here than fairs abroad,” said Hena Kapadia, the founder of the dynamic local gallery Tarq, which sold the majority of its stand—including photographs by the Kolkata-based filmmaker Ronny Sen referencing post-humanism—and rehung around 50% of it.

    Notable sales in the fair’s contemporary section included a Subodh Gupta painting at the Delhi- and Mumbai-based Nature Morte, which placed to a new buyer of Indian-origin based in Europe, for €350,000. The gallery’s director Roma Patel noted that she met new collectors from south India, and diaspora collectors from Los Angeles, as well as existing clients, at the fair.

    In the Modern tent, “some punchy prices” were noted by one auction executive. Works acquired at auction within the past 12 months were flipped for tidy profits, including M F Husain's 1991 Untitled (Horses & Ganesh) at Akar Prakar, bought from Bonhams in December 2025 for £179,000 (equivalent to $234,000) and resold for $600,000, although likely with a hefty discount.

    Sources indicate that subtler gestures of confidence were also observed. Grosvenor Gallery, which counted among its sales a painting by the Sri Lankan Senaka Senanayake for a shade over $100,000, decided not to send out PDFs to its clients prior to the fair. "We haven’t pre-sold anything for the past few fairs—a nice luxury afforded to us by the current market conditions, though it won’t last forever,” remarked the gallery’s director Charlie Moore.

    Art Mumbai takes place at the Mahalaxmi Racecourse.

    In a recent development, with India’s place on the global stage growing, and the predominant art markets of the US, Europe and China remaining relatively muted, international players are circling. Case in point, Frieze's chief executive Simon Fox, and Art Basel’s director of fairs Vincenzo de Bellis and head of VIP Carly Murphy, all attended Art Mumbai for the first time this year. Fox said this was his first India trip for work. Meanwhile, Art Basel’s India VIP representative Shaan Shahani noted that this visit marked the first India trip by Art Basel top brass in a decade.

    Also testing these waters are the 12 international galleries that highlighted at Art Mumbai this year, up from seven last year. Newcomers included the global dealership Perrotin, Richard Saltoun and Niru Ratnam from London, and Rizq from Abu Dhabi, while Lisson, Continua, Ben Brown and Gallery Isabelle all returned from last year. Three international galleries that took part last year did not come back: Rossi & Rossi (Hong Kong); Leila Heller (New York and Dubai) and Saskia Fernando (Colombo).

    Several of these large galleries continued to play it safe, bringing presentations to suit interior design-focused sensibilities and algorithmically informed taste—plenty of reflective surfaces, legible motifs and name brands, such as Ai Weiwei and Anish Kapoor. Lisson's sales topped out at £1.2m, and included two of Kapoor’s signature concave disc sculptures. On the closing day, gallery director Ellie Harrison-Read noted that she had a "good fair, but closing a few more sales could make it great”.

    By and large, galleries that brought subtler or nicher works struggled. Niru Ratnam, which showed small paintings in muted palettes by the late Bengali-British Modernist Amal Ghosh and the British Indian Bhajan Hunjan, did not place a work for the first two days, having pre-sold one painting by Ghosh to cover stand and shipping costs.

    Industry observers note that while both Ghosh and Hunjan are increasingly being reappraised by world leading institutions such as Tate, they are relatively unknown figures in both the UK and India and have proved a tough sell in Mumbai. As one local dealer noted, "I rarely meet collectors here who lead with curiosity or instinct".

    Another litmus test for this market was a painting by Robert Nava, brought by the first-time exhibitor Night gallery from Los Angeles. Nava, who is co-represented by Pace, is a US-based market star whose naive figurative style sharply divides critics. The secondary-market painting, depicting a swimming cat, was tagged at $220,000, a hefty price for a buying pool unfamiliar with his work and where contemporary art by the most established artists rarely exceeds $400,000. It did not sell by the fair’s last day, but the gallery’s director Davida Nemeroff said she had engaged in several serious enquiries, including one local buyer who went home to measure their wall following a conversation on the stand. “We went in pretty blind, and didn’t know what to expect”, she said.

    The gallery did however sell to the Kiran Nadar Museum of Art a $16,000 painting installation by Divya Mehra embossed with words from a speech by Surya Kant, India's chief justice, that sparked the Cockroach Janata Party protests. “We’ve learned that if you don’t bring something vaguely South Asian, or a Picasso, it won’t sell," Nemeroff stated.

    Sources indicate that speaking of Picasso, a 1930s painting by the Spanish master was offered by Ben Brown, carrying a $4.5m price tag—the most expensive work brought to the fair in its four editions. Last year, the gallery indicated a smaller painting by Picasso to Art Mumbai, which did not sell. Rather than being discouraged, gallery director Hugo Cobb decided to double down. “Our feedback was that this market is now discerning enough for quality and it doesn’t want anything second rate,” he said.

    The gallery did not sell the Picasso by the end of the fair, with Cobb attesting to the fact that the very top end of the Indian market still amounts to a handful of collectors. "There are maybe four or five collectors in this country who would buy it, and none of them did." The gallery did, however, sell a monumentally scaled Yoan Capote painting, embedded with fishhooks, for $1m to a local collector. Cobb added that should the gallery return to Art Mumbai, it will focus on bringing high value secondary market material.

    According to recent reports, as many international visitors and exhibitors will have observed, India now has no shortage of deep pocketed buyers, but its tastes remain local and largely conservative. "Collecting in India is largely informed by familiarity," says the adviser Yamini Mehta. "The market here is still not ready for super conceptual stuff.".

    Further factors that keep India's art market more domestically focused than other Asian art hubs include stifling bureaucracy and high taxes involved in shipping works in and out of the country. As the Richard Saltoun director Sakshi Mahajan remarked, "they don't make it easy or cheap to bring in art. Even when it's worth relatively small amounts".

    Recent findings suggest that meanwhile, challenges of black money circulating in the Indian art market persist. As one adviser, speaking anonymously, noted, "many Indians might not want to send money abroad, for fear of those transactions being registered by the RBI (Reserve Bank of India)".

    Sources indicate that india's art market growth indeed appears to be a domestic success story. This is in contrast to its last boom in the 2000s, which was fuelled by speculative buying, often from overseas collectors with no ties to the region.

    While in buzzier Asian art markets like Seoul and Hong Kong, many collectors covet international—usually Western—names at the expense of local talent, India overwhelmingly supports its own artists: representatives from a growing number of upcoming Indian biennials were spotted at the fair, including from the Bengal Biennial and the soon-to-launch Benares Biennial, both of whose artist lists are heavily weighted towards India and the wider South Asian region.

    While India might not yet be ready for a truly international fair or an outpost of a mega gallery, it appears to be building something more valuable: an infrastructural network supporting homegrown talent, which should help to safeguard against another crash when the market eventually enters a soberer period.

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    When procrastination stems from anxiety or fear of failure, use this playbook to help your child get unstuck.

    In a recent development, here’s a familiar scenario: Your student with ADHD sits at the kitchen table, supposedly doing homework. Twenty minutes go by, and you check on their status. Nothing has been accomplished.

    Recent findings suggest that in these moments, your child is invisibly, involuntarily grappling with the Wall of Awful, a term I coined to describe the emotional barrier people confront when faced with draining and/or daunting tasks (homework is a good example). Before your child can engage in work, they must get past this wall of emotions.

    Many parents misinterpret the early warning signs of the Wall. They mistake difficulty starting a task for resistance or defiance. So they double down on being a taskmaster, or, alternatively, they hover and provide too much help. Neither tactic aids their child in the long run.

    [Get This Free Download: What Are Your Teen’s Weakest Executive Functions?].

    Recent findings suggest that instead, I recommend talking about the idea of a Wall of Awful that stands between students and certain tasks. Then, when red flags appear, the Wall becomes the problem, not the kid, enabling the parent and child to problem-solve together.

    In a recent development, the Wall of Awful can affect anyone, but kids with ADHD are especially susceptible because their weak executive functioning skills make completing tasks harder. These struggles, combined with previous failures or fears of failure, add extra emotional bricks to the Wall.

    Here is a quick-start approach that parents can follow to help their student vault the Wall of Awful:.

    Tech Report: The Art of Releasing Resentment in Your ADHD Relationship

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (931 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Additudemag

    ⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • It has been revealed that ADHD can complicate communication, expectations, and daily routines between partners.
    • Recent findings suggest that resentment – the anger, bitterness, and disappointment that build from the feeling we’ve been wronged and treated unfairly over time – is a slowly simmering emotion.
    • According to recent reports, in relationships touched by ADHD, traits like forgetfulness, disorganization, and inconsistent follow-through can hasten these feelings and chip away at intimacy.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    It has been revealed that ADHD can complicate communication, expectations, and daily routines between partners. Here’s how to spot resentment and take steps toward healing and reconnection.

    Recent findings suggest that resentment – the anger, bitterness, and disappointment that build from the feeling we’ve been wronged and treated unfairly over time – is a slowly simmering emotion. Eventually, its toxic burn clouds the way we view our relationship and may even suffocate it.

    According to recent reports, in relationships touched by ADHD, traits like forgetfulness, disorganization, and inconsistent follow-through can hasten these feelings and chip away at intimacy. ADHD partners, in turn, commonly resent their neurotypical partners for misunderstanding the condition and setting unrealistic expectations.

    Resentment is a protective, multilayered emotion that deserves reflection. Follow these steps to gradually untangle the complex feelings you may be harboring about your partner so you can let go of resentment and start healing.

    According to recent reports, resentment is a defense mechanism. Landing a sarcastic comment, giving the silent treatment, or thinking, “Because you didn’t do X, I won’t do Y,” helps us feel in control. These behaviors allow us to avoid confronting difficult feelings and situations, though they eventually backfire and sow deeper resentment. Become clear-eyed about resentment’s function in your relationship so you can opt for more productive responses instead.

    [Get This Free Download: Manage ADHD’s Impact on Your Relationship].

    Recent findings suggest that do you resent your partner for any specific behaviors (or lack thereof)? Peel back the layers on this. Resentment often sits on top of hurt, fear, shame, helplessness, and other uncomfortable feelings. It means that something crucial to you feels threatened, ignored, or unmet.

    For each pain point, think about what lies underneath. What do your partner’s actions trigger in you? What stories are you telling yourself about their behavior? Some examples include:.

    “They leave all the planning to me.”.

    “I feel like a child in this relationship.”.

    “I feel more like a parent than a partner.”.

    “My partner doesn’t respect how I do things or who I am.”.

    “I resent feeling like the family project.”.

    “My partner did something long ago and hasn’t apologized adequately.”.

    [Read: 9 Ways ADHD May Strain Relationships].

    Industry observers note that resolving resentment won’t happen overnight. Acceptance and forgiveness are distinct processes that can help dissolve resentment, but they work differently. If forgiveness feels too “major,” go for the route of acceptance. If one partner keeps forgetting things, for example, asking for forgiveness every time can feel exhausting for both people. Acceptance says: “This is a feature of our relationship that I need to strategy around” rather than “I need to forgive you 50 times.”.

    Miscommunication in neurodiverse relationships often comes from assumptions we make about our partners. We assume they process the world as we do and can read our minds. Review the following steps with your partner to engage in a brief and insightful “learning conversation” about resentments:.

    Speaker: When you seem to be upset and I ask you how you’re doing, you often say you’re feeling “fine.” That makes me feel anxious because I’m not sure it’s true.

    Listener: So you feel anxious when I say I’m fine when you don’t perceive that to be the case… because you think I’m lying to you?

    Speaker: You’re right that I do feel anxious, but I don’t worry so much that you’re lying to me. What I’m concerned about is that you’re not sharing your true self with me.

    Listener: You feel that when I say “I’m fine,” I’m choosing not to open up to you… which makes you feel like I’m not comfortable with you and not invested in our relationship?

    Speaker: Yes, that’s exactly it.

    It has been revealed that what are you willing to relinquish? To decide, get clear about your boundaries. Terri Cole, LCSW, a psychotherapist who specializes in boundaries, asks us to define our values by the following:.

    In a recent development, things that matter to you but are highly flexible and negotiable. Rule of thumb: You’d be okay if you didn’t have them.

    Our most key wishes and goals. They relate to how we envision our life. Compromising on deep desires often leads to resentment.

    Behaviors, values, or situations that are fundamentally unacceptable to you. Crossing them usually means the relationship ends.

    There are no right or wrong answers. A dealbreaker to one person may be a preference to another.

    It has been revealed that consider where your resentments about your partner fit within your system. If you decide that something is a non-issue, create boundaries – rules that you set for yourself, not your partner.

    Example: You’ve decided to let go of resentment about your partner’s untidiness. Your boundary: “What’s on their side of the room is their responsibility to clean.”.

    What Is Considered Upper Middle Class? Income and Net Worth

    📅 22 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 9 min read (1890 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Choosefi

    ⏱️ ~9 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Where Americans fall on the income spectrum — Pew Research Center 2026 data.
    • National median household income — the midpoint dividing upper and lower halves.
    • households classified as upper income by Pew Research.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    What's your FI number? Calculate it in 60 seconds.

    The one number that changes everything.

    Where Americans fall on the income spectrum — Pew Research Center 2026 data.

    National median household income — the midpoint dividing upper and lower halves.

    Share of U.S. households classified as upper income by Pew Research.

    How much location can shift income class thresholds between cheapest and costliest metros.

    Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

    Industry observers note that the most widely cited framework for income classes comes from the Pew Research Center, which uses a straightforward formula based on the national median household income. Pew defines three tiers:.

    Using the most recent Census Bureau data with a national median household income of approximately $84,900, the thresholds for a three-person household look like this:.

    The "upper middle class" label is not an official Pew category — it is a colloquial term most commonly used to describe the band between the middle of the middle class and the beginning of the upper class. Think of it as the top quarter of the middle-income range through the entry point of the upper-income range: households earning roughly $106,000 to $169,800.

    These definitions are adjusted for household size using an equivalence scale. A single person needs less income than a family of five to achieve the same standard of living. Pew adjusts all income figures to a three-person household equivalent, which is why the thresholds you see in different sources sometimes vary — they may be using different household sizes as their reference point.

    In a recent development, national income thresholds are useful starting points, but they obscure a critical reality: the cost of living varies so dramatically across the United States that the same income places you in different classes depending on where you live. Pew Research's cost-of-living adjusted data reveals just how stark these differences are.

    It has been revealed that A household earning $150,000 in Jackson, Mississippi — where the cost of living is roughly 83% of the national average — has purchasing power equivalent to about $180,700 nationally. That same $150,000 in San Francisco, where costs run about 180% of the national average, has purchasing power equivalent to only $83,300 — technically middle class by Pew's national definitions.

    This explains why so many households earning $150,000 to $200,000 in coastal cities feel middle class despite technically being upper-income by national standards. They are not wrong — their lived experience of housing costs, childcare, and taxes genuinely consumes their income at the same rate as middle-income households in lower-cost areas.

    Recent findings suggest that income class and wealth class are not the same thing. The Federal Reserve's Survey of Consumer Finances reveals that high income does not automatically translate to high net worth. Many upper-income households carry large mortgages, student loans, and car payments that consume much of their earnings. Meanwhile, some middle-income households with high savings rates accumulate substantial wealth over time.

    According to recent reports, the FI community lives in this gap. A household earning $90,000 that saves 50% of their income and invests consistently will have a higher net worth within 10-15 years than a household earning $250,000 that saves 5%. Income determines your ceiling; savings rate determines your trajectory. This is why ChooseFI focuses on savings rate and investable net worth as the primary metrics of financial progress — not income class labels.

    The financial independence community occupies a unique position in the income class framework. Survey data from FIRE-focused communities suggests the median household income among FI seekers is roughly $130,000 to $160,000 — placing most in the upper-middle-class to lower-upper-income range. However, successful FI stories span the entire income spectrum, from teachers earning $55,000 to tech executives earning $500,000.

    What distinguishes FI community members from their income peers is not what they earn but what they keep. While the average upper-middle-class household saves 8-12% of income, FI-path households in the same income range typically save 40-60%. This results in net worth accumulation that dramatically outpaces their income class peers.

    It has been revealed that the lesson from this comparison is that income class labels describe your earning power, but they say nothing about your financial trajectory. A middle-income household on the FI path will typically surpass the net worth of upper-income households who spend freely. The FI framework redefines "class" around financial freedom rather than consumption — your class is determined not by what you can afford to buy, but by how many years of expenses your investments can cover.

    Income class definitions use household income, which combines the earnings of all adults in a home. This creates a nuance worth understanding: a dual-income household where each partner earns $75,000 has the same household income ($150,000) as a single-earner household at that level, but the dual-income household often faces higher total costs (two commutes, potentially more childcare) and different tax treatment. When evaluating where you fall, always use your total household income before taxes and compare to thresholds adjusted for your household size.

    The distinction between wealth and income is the foundation of financial independence. Your income class describes your present earning power. Your net worth describes your accumulated financial freedom. The FI community's central insight is that you can move from any income class to financial independence by controlling the gap between what you earn and what you spend — and investing the difference consistently in low-cost index funds over time.

    Free calculators, a personalized FI roadmap, and a community of 25K+ on the same journey.

    Sources indicate that whether you are middle class, upper middle class, or upper class by any definition, your path to financial independence depends on one number: your savings rate. A middle-income household saving 50% of their income will reach FI decades before an upper-income household saving 5%. Focus on growing the gap between what you earn and what you spend — the class label takes care of itself.

    Take the next step with your finances.

    Use these calculators to see where you stand on your FI journey.

    Find out how much you need to reach financial independence.

    See if your current investments can coast to your retirement target.

    Your savings rate matters more than returns. See where you are.

    Add up all pre-tax income for your household — wages, self-employment, investment income, and any other sources. Compare to the Pew thresholds adjusted for your household size. For a three-person household, middle income is $56,600 to $169,800.

    Use a cost-of-living calculator to adjust your income to the national equivalent. A $120,000 income in a city with 130% cost-of-living has the same purchasing power as $92,300 nationally. This adjusted number is a more honest reflection of your class position.

    Your net worth — assets minus liabilities — is a better indicator of financial health than income alone. The median net worth for upper-middle-class households is roughly $465,000. If you are above that with a lower income, you are wealthier than your income class suggests.

    Divide your annual savings (including employer retirement contributions) by your gross income. The national average is under 5%. The FI community targets 40-60%. Your savings rate is the single most important predictor of when you will reach financial independence.

    In a recent development, multiply your annual spending by 25 to find your FI number (based on the 4% safe withdrawal rate). Then use your current savings rate and existing net worth to estimate how many years until you reach that number. This timeline matters more than any income class label.

    According to Pew Research, upper-income households earn more than double the national median household income. For a three-person household in 2026, that threshold is approximately $169,800. However, this varies significantly by location — in San Francisco, you would need roughly $306,000 to have the same purchasing power as $169,800 nationally.

    Upper middle class generally describes households in the top 20-30% of earners but below the top 5% — roughly $106,000 to $169,800 for a three-person household. Upper class typically refers to households above $169,800 (top 19%). The top 5% begins at roughly $280,000 and the top 1% at approximately $590,000. These are income-based definitions and do not account for net worth.

    By national standards, $200,000 household income places you in the upper-income category (above the $169,800 threshold for a three-person household). However, in high-cost cities like San Francisco, Fresh York, or Boston, $200,000 has purchasing power equivalent to roughly $111,000 to $130,000 nationally — solidly middle class in terms of lived experience.

    In a recent development, the Federal Reserve Survey of Consumer Finances shows the median net worth of upper-income households is approximately $805,400. The top 10% of U.S. households by net worth have $1.9 million or more, and the top 1% have $11.1 million or more. Net worth is a more meaningful measure of financial security than income because it reflects accumulated wealth, not just current earning power.

    Lifestyle inflation is the primary reason. Many households increase their spending in lockstep with income increases — larger homes, newer cars, private schools, premium vacations — leaving little margin for savings. A household earning $300,000 that spends $290,000 accumulates wealth more slowly than one earning $100,000 that spends $50,000. The FI community calls this the HENRY problem: High Earner, Not Rich Yet.

    According to recent reports, pew Research adjusts income thresholds using an equivalence scale based on household size. A single person needs roughly $56,600 to be middle income (the lower bound), while a family of five needs roughly $126,500 for the same standard of living. Larger households need more income to achieve the same class designation because they have more people sharing the resources.

    Income class labels provide useful context for understanding where you stand relative to other American households, but they are a poor measure of financial health. Plenty of upper-income households are one job loss away from financial crisis because they spend everything they earn, while many middle-income households on the FI path have built net worth that places them in the top 10% of all Americans. The framework that matters most is not whether you are middle class, upper middle class, or upper class — it is whether the gap between your income and your spending is large enough to build financial independence within a timeline that matters to you. Focus on three numbers: your savings rate, your investable net worth, and your FI number. Everything else is a label that describes your present circumstances, not your financial future.

    Industry News: Miami artists’ Art Basel boycott campaign calls for alternatives to fair week’s commercial model

    📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1151 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Theartnewspaper

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • As Art Basel Miami Beach prepares to return to the city, a group of local artists and organisers is asking the Miami art community to reconsider its relationship with the busy week of fairs that takes over the city every December.
    • It has been revealed that in a city whose international cultural profile has become virtually inseparable from the Art Basel brand, the boycott poses a difficult question: can Miami’s arts economy sustain its local creative community without depending so heavily on the machinery of a global art fair?
    • “We realise that in order to refuse to take part in something as intertwined and culturally impactful as Art Basel, you really have to start building an alternative,” notes misael soto, an artist and founder of Artists 4 Artists Miami.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    As Art Basel Miami Beach prepares to return to the city, a group of local artists and organisers is asking the Miami art community to reconsider its relationship with the busy week of fairs that takes over the city every December. The grassroots collective Artists 4 Artists Miami declared intends for its “Art Basel Boycott” at a protest outside the Miami Beach Convention Center at the end of last year’s edition of the Switzerland-based fair. Now, after a year of preparation, the collective is launching its first campaign, inviting local artists, curators, gallerists, collectors and residents to reconsider their participation in Miami Art Week’s fairs while building alternatives rooted in the community.

    It has been revealed that in a city whose international cultural profile has become virtually inseparable from the Art Basel brand, the boycott poses a difficult question: can Miami’s arts economy sustain its local creative community without depending so heavily on the machinery of a global art fair? Organisers are not calling for a blanket rejection of Miami Art Week or even its tentpole event. Instead, organisers envision a longer-term effort to challenge the economic and political structures surrounding the fair and redirect attention toward local artists, independent galleries and experimental programming.

    “We realise that in order to refuse to take part in something as intertwined and culturally impactful as Art Basel, you really have to start building an alternative,” notes misael soto, an artist and founder of Artists 4 Artists Miami.

    Sources indicate that the campaign grew out of the collective’s broader efforts to connect cultural work with other grassroots struggles. After spending much of 2025 supporting campaigns led by other organisations, Artists 4 Artists Miami began considering how it could mobilise its own community. Its participation in protests organised by Jewish Voice for Peace and other groups opposing the war in Gaza helped crystallise the idea, soto claims, prompting organisers to examine the connections between the art market, housing affordability, labour conditions, and the companies that benefit from the fair.

    For soto, Art Basel has become a focal point for these overlapping concerns. The fair generates significant economic activity, but the group questions how much of that value reaches Miami’s working artists and residents, particularly as the city becomes increasingly expensive. The group also points to the environmental and infrastructural costs of hosting an international event, and to the political and corporate interests associated with some of its major partners and investors.

    In a recent development, those concerns extend to the fair’s relationship with the city itself; soto points to a recent Miami Beach Commission decision concerning Art Basel’s rental agreement for the Miami Beach Convention Center, which reduced the fair’s rent from nearly $1m to around $500,000 and committed the equivalent of an additional $300,000 in public funds toward first-responder and security costs. The group questions whether the benefits the fair brings to the community justify the public resources devoted to it.

    According to recent reports, and yet, as the Artists 4 Artists Miami organisers acknowledge, Art Basel is deeply embedded in Miami’s cultural identity and economy. For many artists and arts workers, Miami Art Week provides essential income through art handling, installation, production and other contract jobs, while offering a smaller number opportunities to exhibit their work. Local galleries rely on the annual influx of collectors, press and visitors, and cultural institutions benefit from the attention and potential donor relationships the week brings.

    According to recent reports, “Art Basel Miami Beach has been a committed partner to Miami Beach and its creative community for more than two decades, supporting local artists and organisations through cultural programming, educational initiatives and opportunities for artistic exchange,” a spokesperson for Art Basel tells The Art Newspaper. “The fair also generates significant economic activity across the region, benefiting local businesses and workers in a wide range of sectors.”.

    According to local officials, the 2025 edition of Art Basel Miami Beach generated nearly $60m in economic impact for the city of Miami Beach, and $570m in economic impact for Miami-Dade County. The fair has consistently included several South Florida galleries as exhibitors, and every year the city of Miami Beach acquires a work from the fair for its public art collection.

    It has been revealed that ariel Lynch, an artist and educator who has lived in the city for four years, signed the Artists 4 Artists Miami pledge despite recognising the tensions inherent in the campaign. Lynch says the fair offers substantial economic benefits to established galleries and collectors while providing comparatively few exhibition opportunities for local artists.

    “Miami deserves more than institutions like Art Basel Miami Beach,” Lynch notes. She prepares to spend Miami Art Week visiting local galleries, events and experimental exhibitions instead of attending the main fair, while introducing students to the city’s year-round art scene.

    Industry observers note that still, Lynch acknowledges the difficult position facing those who depend on Art Basel for their livelihoods. For workers already struggling to make ends meet, declining paid work during Miami Art Week may not be financially feasible. That is a dilemma soto is also mindful of: the fairs have helped pay their bills and enabled them to travel internationally, but they believe the short-term benefits can obscure longer-term costs, including overwork, underappreciated labour and environmental strain.

    The “Art Basel Boycott” pledge is designed to accommodate different levels of participation. Signatories must select at least one commitment: not attending Art Basel Miami Beach, not exhibiting work at the fair, not exhibiting during Miami Art Week or withholding their labour from the fair. They can also choose commitments aimed at supporting alternatives, allowing participants to assess what is realistic given their circumstances.

    Sources indicate that as of this writing, the campaign had collected 21 signatures through an online form hosted on the collective’s website. Organisers are contacting local cultural and political organisations, particularly grassroots groups, to seek endorsements and establish partnerships. One existing partner is Panamía, a local network connecting businesses, creatives and residents. Artists 4 Artists Miami is also exploring programming in conjunction with a Panamía gathering and art print fair planned for Miami Art Week.

    It has been revealed that beyond events, the collective hopes to establish a mutual-support network that could help pledge signatories navigate the financial consequences of opting out of Miami Art Week. That would entail connecting artists and organisations with local resources, soto says, including food assistance and other forms of mutual aid.

    According to recent reports, for the boycott’s organisers and signatories, success will not necessarily be measured by a signature count or an immediate impact on the fair. Instead, they hope the campaign will encourage a gradual shift in how Miami’s cultural producers and workers understand their economic and political influence.

    “If a year from now we see that much more alternative and locally focused programming happening outside of Art Week,” soto states, “that would be a huge victory.”.

    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Almost four in five people with chronic migraine have low levels of this vitamin.
    • Almost four in five people with chronic migraine have low levels of this vitamin.
    • Frequent headaches are linked to lower vitamin D levels.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Almost four in five people with chronic migraine have low levels of this vitamin.

    Almost four in five people with chronic migraine have low levels of this vitamin.

    Frequent headaches are linked to lower vitamin D levels.

    People with chronic migraine have lower levels than those with occasional migraines or no headache disorder.

    Lower vitamin D is also associated with greater muscle tenderness.

    The vitamin helps muscles and nerves function, making it relevant to understanding pain.

    One possibility is that low levels amplify sensitivity to pain, although this remains an explanation to investigate.

    The research compared around 150 adults, divided equally between chronic migraine, episodic migraine and a group without headache disorders.

    Blood tests showed low vitamin D in 78 percent of the chronic migraine group, compared with 60 percent of those with episodic migraine and 46 percent of the comparison group.

    Average levels were lowest in chronic migraine and highest among those without headaches.

    Chronic migraine means headaches on at least 15 days a month for more than three months, with migraine features on at least eight days.

    These headaches can change in character, even within the same day, and can include pain resembling tension headaches.

    Lower vitamin D levels were associated with more tenderness when muscles were pressed.

    The researchers suggest that muscular discomfort and changes in pain processing could interact, potentially helping sustain headaches.

    However, the association could also run in the opposite direction: people with migraine may spend less time outdoors because of light sensitivity or fatigue.

    The findings do not establish that supplements prevent migraines.

    Vitamin D’s established functions extend beyond maintaining strong bones.

    It helps the body absorb calcium, supports muscle movement and allows nerves to carry messages between the brain and the body.

    Deficiency can cause a condition called osteomalacia in adults, involving bone pain and muscle weakness.

    The body produces vitamin D when sunlight reaches the skin, while food provides another source.

    Oily fish, including salmon and mackerel, are among the best natural sources, while egg yolks contain smaller amounts.

    Some breakfast cereals and other foods are fortified with the vitamin.

    People who rarely expose their skin to sunlight can have more difficulty obtaining enough.

    A blood test measures vitamin D status, helping distinguish a nutritional shortage from symptoms with other possible explanations.

    The study was published in the journal Cephalalgia Reports (Prakash et al., 2026).

    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    STUDIO HERRSTRÃM rebuilds the Milkshake brand identity around car culture, a redrawn splash mark, high-vis color and road signs.

    Milkshake is a Stockholm label, a division of Sony Music Entertainment founded in 2019, and its new identity starts in a car. The name was suggested on a car ride, milestones happened in cars, and new music was taken for a car test. The old splash is still there, redrawn as a rounded, blended symbol that reads like metal and liquid merging, and the wordmark runs through it with a zigzag cut that splits Milkshake into two stacked hits. On the posters the name fills the frame until the letters stop being text and start being the picture: acid yellow Milksh across the top, shake across the bottom.

    The type system is Gates, a neo-grotesque from Contextype, shown in the specimen with arrows, asterisks, circled letters and roman numerals on a mauve field. The wordmark itself leans forward, its letters cut on a slant that matches the splash, and the supporting lockups borrow their logic from car window stickers and milk carton nutrition labels: small blocks of capitals that hold track names, release dates and the p-line symbol without breaking the grid.

    In a recent development, the system proves itself on the objects it touches. A high-vis vest carries the full lockup on its back in black on acid yellow, with reflective bands borrowed from road markings. A neon green acrylic cube hangs outside the shopfront with the black wordmark on its face. A blender wears the whole icon set as stickers: the machine that makes the drink becomes the merch.

    Color does the rest. Acid yellow is the signal color, while neon pink and soft lilac take the flavor cues and black keeps the contrast high. The same palette runs the subway poster for Tove Lo's single Me/You (always and forever), dated 18.09.26. Linn Wexell, founder and creative director of Milkshake, indicates the creative work was smart and on point and the visuals stunning.

    #160817. What Does Gen Z Think About Political Polarization?

    What Does Gen Z Think About Political Polarization?

    📅 27 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1264 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Berkeley

    ⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
    📖 0% read
    💡 Key Takeaways
    • Sources indicate that polarization is a fact of political life in the U.S.
    • In a recent development, “Polarization doesn’t seem to be a fixed trend in Gen Z’s minds,” remarked Jadon Urogdy.
    • Urogdy and his classmates also found that Gen Z, which is the cohort born between 1997 and 2012 and considered the first true “digital natives,” is more comfortable than their elders in having a political conversation online—findings that suggest they may be more reachable and receptive to online interventions aimed at reducing polarization.
    📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

    Sources indicate that polarization is a fact of political life in the U.S. today. Gen Z, however, is less inclined than older generations to view it as a permanent fixture in American politics, according to research by students in the Stanford political science course Democracy in the Balance: Polarization and the Road Ahead. Students found that Gen Z is more optimistic than any other age group about the possibility of bridging the political divide in America.

    In a recent development, “Polarization doesn’t seem to be a fixed trend in Gen Z’s minds,” remarked Jadon Urogdy. “We have a bright future. Our identities and views are still malleable, and that’s exactly why this moment matters so much.”.

    Urogdy and his classmates also found that Gen Z, which is the cohort born between 1997 and 2012 and considered the first true “digital natives,” is more comfortable than their elders in having a political conversation online—findings that suggest they may be more reachable and receptive to online interventions aimed at reducing polarization.

    Sources indicate that urogdy’s results were among many findings from Democracy in the Balance: Polarization and the Road Ahead, a spring quarter course taught by Ashley Fabrizio, a Stanford alum and head of research at the nonpartisan think tank More in Common. Working with Fabrizio and her team, students created and conducted a nationally representative survey of 1,610 U.S. adults that oversampled Gen Z to provide a more granular look into their political attitudes and opinions.

    Industry observers note that fabrizio, who has taught the course for three years, has found that working with students surfaces concerns that standard polling may miss. “If we want to know what Gen Z’s political beliefs and attitudes are, we should let our students, as members of Gen Z, use their intuition to decide what matters in a survey,” Fabrizio explained.

    Industry observers note that working in small groups, students were allocated several minutes of survey time to explore topics such as the political influence of online content promoting masculinity—aka the “manosphere”—the religious revival in Gen Z’s lives, and their beliefs about the American dream. Fabrizio guided students step by step through survey design, showing them how to craft research questions, field the survey, analyze data, and, finally, present their findings.

    Students also examined the academic literature on polarization’s effects in American politics, such as how it contributes to political gridlock, drives support for political violence, and erodes trust in American institutions.

    “There are many legitimate divisions in politics over competing policies and values, but polarization often drives us apart unnecessarily,” noted Fabrizio. “Young Americans will have to find their own ways of bridging partisan differences and overcoming misconceptions about one another. I hope this class helps students see the value of doing so and gives them a sense of agency in addressing polarization.”.

    Natalia Galperin was excited about the opportunity to run her own study from start to finish, a first for the Stanford undergrad majoring in psychology. She also wanted to expand on her prior work as a research assistant for political scientist Shanto Iyengar in his Political Communication Lab, where she studied the effects of negative political campaign ads.

    For her research project, Galperin examined the role of social media in inflating Gen Z’s hostility toward people from the opposing political party, a phenomenon political scientists call “affective polarization.”.

    “We thought Gen Z would be more polarized and misinformed because we get so much of our news on social media compared to older generations,” Galperin remarked.

    What she and her classmates found reveals a more complicated picture.

    While Gen Z respondents who mentioned they used social media daily or almost daily were more likely to dislike the opposing party, their scores were almost identical to those of other generations.

    “We found that greater social media engagement is generally linked to more polarized views of political parties, and the effect is seen at similar rates across all generations, not just Gen Z,” mentioned Galperin, who will be interning with More In Common this summer.

    Practices to help campus communities connect across lines of race, faith, ideology, and more.

    Galperin also wanted to know whether social media deepens the divide between what Gen Z thinks people from the other side believe versus what they actually think, a phenomenon known as “perception gaps.” In testing people’s perceptions on immigration, she found that Gen Z did not appear to hold wildly distorted views about the other side—findings that push back against the familiar narrative that being online warps a person’s perceptions of politics.

    Taken together, actively using social media seems to harden Gen Z’s feelings more than it distorts basic facts.

    The class also found a wide range of political viewpoints, including differences between Gen Z who identified as Democrats and Republicans.

    For example, in Urogdy’s project, he and his teammates found that those who were the most confident that polarization can be reduced identified as conservatives and Republicans, while liberals and Democrats believed the opposite—a finding that Urogdy said tracks with prior research: A person’s view of government depends on whether or not their political party is in control.

    Galperin’s team also found lower levels of affective polarization among Republicans and Gen Z overall, and Democrats who reported actively using social media daily have higher perception gaps on immigration-related problems than average.

    Another student team’s project revealed further complexities. They found that many Gen Z respondents are more likely than other generations to attribute problems like the affordability crisis to systemic failures in democracy itself rather than to specific policies or leaders. In their data, a notable share of young people noted the system itself “is not capable of doing its job,” signaling a deeper, structural disillusionment.

    Sources indicate that “I think we’re all exhausted by the political system,” Urogdy said. “There’s this underlying feeling that what we want isn’t being translated into tangible change, and I think that there’s this overall feeling that instead of having animosity towards people across the aisle, there’s an animosity towards the system itself.”.

    Urogdy is pragmatic about what comes next.

    It has been revealed that “We can’t say polarization will disappear if we will it away,” said Urogdy, who is majoring in political science. Now, he feels he has a better understanding of what kinds of solutions matter. If people are disillusioned with the system, surface-level fixes—such as messaging—won’t last, he said. Efforts need to be ongoing. “If Gen Z is still one of the most reachable generations, the answer is sustained civic engagement, where we can rebuild trust in the system while working to reform it. We have a long path ahead,” said Urogdy, who said he is optimistic.

    In a recent development, fabrizio, too, is hopeful. “Gen Z is inheriting a polarized nation, but they are inheriting deep wells of democratic vitality, as well,” Fabrizio said. “America has a long history of self-government, a robust civil society, and communities that remain deeply committed to democratic values. Gen Z has high standards for our democracy, but living up to them is within reach. I hope older generations will listen and be inspired by Gen Z’s vision for the American dream.”.

She attained an M.A. in Media, Culture, & Communication from NYU and a B.Sc. in Sociology from LSE. She was previously the digital communications manager for the Division of Social Sciences at UC Santa Cruz.

    #160816. 60 mindful Upcoming Year's resolution ideas to try in 2027

    📅 12 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 26m • 📚 Deep Dive (5116 w)
